Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

stat_p_nonsig.report: Meta-scientific research has shown nonsignificant p values are commonly misinterpreted. It is incorrect to infer that there is 'no effect', 'no difference', or that groups are 'the same' after p > 0.05. It is possible that there is a true non-zero effect, but that the study did not detect it. Make sure your inference acknowledges that it is possible that there is a non-zero effect. It is correct to include the effect is 'not significantly' different, although this just restates that p > 0.05. Metacheck does not yet analyze automatically whether sentences which include non-significant p-values are correct, but we recommend manually checking the sentences below for possible misinterpreted non-significant p values. ```{r} #| echo: false # table data -------------------------------------- table <- structure(list(Text = c("p = .995", "p = .209", "p = .142"), Sentence = c("By contrast, the interaction between test and numerical ratio did not significantly improve model fit, χ²(1) < 0.01, p = .995.", "Baseline 8 versus 4 trials did not show a significant overall side bias, z = 1.26, p = .209.", "A categorical model including numerosity as a factor also improved fit relative to the intercept-only model, χ²(3) = 34.74, p < .001, but did not improve fit beyond the linear-trend model, χ²(2) = 3.91, p = .142." )), row.names = c(NA, -3L), class = c("tbl_df", "tbl", "data.frame" )) # display table ----------------------------------- metacheck::report_table(table, c(0.1, 0.9), 10, FALSE) ``` ::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"} For metascientific articles demonstrating the rate of misinterpretations of non-significant results is high, see: Aczel B, Palfi B, Szollosi A, Kovacs M, Szaszi B, Szecsi P, Zrubka M, Gronau Q, van den Bergh D, Wagenmakers E (2018). “Quantifying Support for the Null Hypothesis in Psychology: An Empirical Investigation.” Advances in Methods and Practices in Psychological Science, 1(3), 357–366. doi:10.1177/2515245918773742. Murphy S, Merz R, Reimann L, Fernández A (2025). “Nonsignificance misinterpreted as an effect’s absence in psychology: Prevalence and temporal analyses.” Royal Society Open Science, 12(3), 242167. doi:10.1098/rsos.242167. For educational material on preventing the misinterpretation of p values, see [Improving Your Statistical Inferences](https://lakens.github.io/statistical_inferences/01-pvalue.html#sec-misconception1). :::

info.title: Mice (Mus musculus) discriminate static dot arrays differing in relative numerosity but show limited evidence of a magnitude-related bias in side choice

text.text: We investigated whether mice can discriminate static dot arrays differing in relative numerosity and whether stimulus magnitude influences side choice.

In Experiment 1, mice were trained in a touchscreen-equipped operant-conditioning chamber to select the larger of two dot arrays (8 vs. 4) and then completed reinforced test blocks that introduced untrained numerosity pairs and stimulus manipulations of continuous physical variables.
Mice showed evidence of transfer to novel comparisons, and accuracy varied systematically with the numerical ratio, consistent with Weber-like scaling.
Accuracy remained above chance with open-circle displays, but performance declined when cumulative surface area was equated and when discrete item structure was disrupted by phase scrambling.
These findings indicate that mice can learn and generalize relative numerosity discriminations, although their performance was also influenced by correlated continuous visual properties.
Thus, the results do not establish stimulus control by numerosity independently of these properties.

In Experiment 2, we examined whether stimulus magnitude influenced side choice under noncontingent probe conditions, in which identical dot arrays were presented simultaneously on the left and right sides of the screen.
Under these conditions, the probability of choosing the left side increased with numerosity at the group level.
Together, these results demonstrate that mice can learn and generalize discriminations between static dot arrays and provide limited evidence of a magnitude-related bias in side choice.

The ability to discriminate magnitudes, including discrete numerosities, allows animals to make adaptive decisions in contexts such as foraging, predator avoidance, mate choice, and social interaction (Macchinizzi et al., 2025).

Despite their central role in behavioral neuroscience, laboratory mice (Mus musculus) remain underrepresented in studies examining numerosity judgments based on purely visual, static displays.

Existing evidence indicates that rodents can process numerosity across a variety of experimental paradigms, but much of the mouse literature has relied on sequential events or response-based counting rather than on simultaneous visual arrays (Meck & Church, 1983; Berkay et al., 2016; Çavdaroğlu & Balcı, 2016; Gür et al., 2021; Light et al., 2019).

text.text: In sequential paradigms, numerosity is inferred from the accumulation of actions or events over time, which limits direct comparison with studies of visual numerosity discrimination using static displays.

By contrast, studies in rats have demonstrated ratio-sensitive performance in twochoice discrimination tasks using simultaneous visual stimuli (Cox & Montrose, 2016), and striped field mice (Apodemus agrarius) can discriminate relative numerosity from dot arrays presented at spatially distinct locations within an arena (Reznikova et al., 2019).

text.text: Establishing reliable visual numerosity discrimination is a prerequisite for addressing broader questions about how numerical magnitude is represented and used by animals.
Beyond discrimination itself, a major open question is whether numerical magnitude systematically influences spatial responding, as predicted by accounts that posit a mental number line.

In humans, the Spatial-Numerical Association of Response Codes (SNARC) effect describes systematic links between numerical magnitude and spatial responses (Dehaene et al., 1993; Toomarian & Hubbard, 2018).
text.formatted: In humans, the Spatial-Numerical Association of Response Codes (SNARC) effect describes systematic links between numerical magnitude and spatial responses <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Dehaene et al., 1993;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">Toomarian & Hubbard, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Evidence for analogous magnitude-space associations in nonhuman animals is mixed and appears to depend on species and task structure (Rugani & Rosa-Salva, 2021).
text.formatted: Evidence for analogous magnitude-space associations in nonhuman animals is mixed and appears to depend on species and task structure <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Rugani & Rosa-Salva, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Robust group-level spatial-numerical biases have been reported in chicks and honeybees under some procedures (Rugani et al., 2015 (Rugani et al., , 2020;; Giurfa et al., 2022), whereas other studies have found individual-level associations that vary in direction across subjects, as observed in pigeons and other birds (Lazareva et al., 2020).

text.text: Evidence from primates and fish has also been mixed, with some studies reporting no reliable directional biases (Triki & Bshary, 2018; Beran et al., 2019), whereas others have demonstrated magnitude-related spatial associations in rhesus macaques (Rugani et al., 2024).

text.text: Interpretation of magnitude-space effects in nonhuman animals therefore remains debated, with concerns about task dependence and about inferring a unitary mental number line from spatial response biases alone (Fragaszy, 2019; Eccher et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Interpretation of magnitude-space effects in nonhuman animals therefore remains debated, with concerns about task dependence and about inferring a unitary mental number line from spatial response biases alone <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Fragaszy, 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b12">Eccher et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: Crucially, any test of spatial-numerical associations presupposes that animals extract numerical magnitude from the visual stimuli themselves; this requirement has not been sufficiently validated in laboratory mice using static arrays, where performance may instead be supported by nonnumerical visual properties that covary with numerosity, such as cumulative surface area, density, element size, and spatial configuration.
A prominent candidate mechanism for visual numerosity judgments is the approximate number system, which supports analog magnitude representations and is behaviorally characterized by Weber's law.

Under Weber scaling, discriminability depends on numerical ratio rather than absolute difference, so comparisons with coarser ratios are easier than those with finer ratios (Piazza et al., 2004; Nieder & Dehaene, 2009).
text.formatted: Under Weber scaling, discriminability depends on numerical ratio rather than absolute difference, so comparisons with coarser ratios are easier than those with finer ratios <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">(Piazza et al., 2004;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b29">Nieder & Dehaene, 2009)</ref>.

text.text: Demonstrating ratio dependence therefore provides a principled benchmark for assessing whether animals extract numerical magnitude from visual arrays and for validating stimulus conditions before testing spatialnumerical associations.
Static dot arrays, however, intrinsically covary numerosity with continuous visual dimensions such as total area, density, and spatial configuration.

A convincing assessment in rodents therefore requires testing untrained numerosity pairs, analyzing Weber-like scaling, and applying stimulus manipulations designed to reduce or disrupt nonnumerical cues.

In the present study, numerosity refers to the number of discrete items in a display, quantity is used more broadly to refer to discrete and continuous stimulus dimensions together, and magnitude is reserved for broader representational or spatial-mapping interpretations.
In static dot-array tasks, numerosity covaries with continuous visual dimensions such as total area and spatial configuration.

Accordingly, we first examined whether mice could discriminate relative numerosity in static dot arrays and whether performance showed ratio dependence while remaining sensitive to correlated nonnumerical visual cues.
We then examined whether stimulus magnitude was associated with side choice under noncontingent probe conditions.
Six male C57BL/6N mice (Japan SLC, Japan) were used.

The animals arrived at 8 weeks of age and were group housed in a standard plastic cage (182 × 260 × 128 mm) with paper bedding (Alpha-Dri, Shepherd Specialty Papers) under a 12:12-hr light-dark cycle (lights on from 06:00 to 18:00).
Behavioral testing began after a 2-week acclimation period.
Mice were maintained on a food-restricted regimen throughout the study.

Mean body weight decreased from 23.9 g (range = 22.0-25.0 g) to 21.6 g (range = 19.5-23.0 g) following food restriction and was subsequently maintained by providing daily food supplements (typically 1.75 g per mouse) in addition to the food reinforcers earned during task sessions.
Water was available ad libitum in the home cages.
All testing was conducted during the light phase.
The sample size was comparable to sample sizes used in previous touchscreen studies of visual discrimination in mice.
No a priori power analysis was conducted.
Testing was conducted in an operant conditioning chamber (Med Associates, ENV-307W) housed within a soundattenuating enclosure (ENV-022V).
The chamber measured 21.6 × 18.0 × 17.8 cm (length × width × height) and had a metal frame, transparent Perspex walls, and a stainlesssteel grid floor.
A pellet dispenser (Bio-Serv F0071-J50) located outside the chamber delivered 20-mg food pellets to a centrally positioned magazine on the rear wall.
The magazine was equipped with a light-emitting diode and a photocell detector (ENV-303HDW) to monitor head entries.
A houselight (1.0 A) and a tone generator (ENV-324W) were mounted on the rear panel.
The front wall was fitted with a 10.4-in. touchscreen monitor (1,024 × 768 pixels; K-Limbic Systems) with an infrared touch frame.
A black acrylic mask covered the monitor, leaving two square response windows (7.5 × 7.5 cm) visible, each positioned 2 cm above the floor.
A horizontal bar fence below the screen restricted access to these response areas.

All components, including the lights, magazine, tone generator, pellet dispenser, and detec-tors, were controlled via a digital input/output board (Velleman K8055) connected to a Lenovo ThinkPad T440p running custom software written in Visual Basic 6 (Microsoft).

Each stimulus consisted of a white-on-black dot array.
The elements were white circles (4.3 mm in diameter) displayed against a black background.
Mice viewed the screen from approximately 2.5-10 cm during choice responses (Figure 2).

Behavioral measurements indicate that C57BL/6 mice have a spatial visual acuity of approximately 0.5 cycles/degree (Prusky et al., 2000), suggesting that the highcontrast dots used here were sufficiently large to be visually resolved even at the longest estimated viewing distance.

Dot centers were constrained to an invisible 4 × 4 grid, yielding 16 possible locations.
For each numerosity, four arrangements were pseudorandomly generated in advance by assigning dots to nonoverlapping positions on the 4 × 4 grid.
These fixed arrangements were combined into four predetermined 8-versus-4 stimulus pairs and used throughout training.
Each stimulus pair was presented in both left-right assignments across the two response windows, with the rewarded numerosity appearing equally often in the left and right windows.
During the test phases, untrained numerosity pairs and stimulus manipulations were introduced in reinforced test blocks to assess performance beyond the trained 8 versus 4 comparison.
In one manipulation, the arrays were rendered as open-circle displays to alter element appearance while preserving numerosity.
In another, cumulative surface area was equated between the two arrays on each trial by scaling element size, thereby reducing total area as a correlated cue.

In a third manipulation, phase-scrambled versions of the dot arrays were generated by randomizing the phase spectrum while preserving the amplitude spectrum, thus preserving global luminance and spatial-frequency content while disrupting discrete item structure.

This experiment examined whether mice could learn to select the larger of two dot arrays and generalize this discrimination across novel numerosity pairs and visual manipulations, and whether their performance followed Weber's law.
Mice were first habituated to the testing chamber and trained to retrieve 20-mg food pellets from the central mag-azine (magazine training).
They were then shaped to make a nose-touch response to a white circle (2.0 cm in diameter) presented on the touchscreen.
Once this response was performed reliably, the stimulus location was randomized across trials.
A self-start procedure was then introduced.
Each trial began with a blinking magazine light (250-ms interval), and a head entry into the magazine triggered the simultaneous presentation of two stimuli, one in each response window.

These pretraining steps, including magazine training, autoshaping, shaping of screen-directed responses, and the self-start procedure, followed the methods described in detail by Goto and Hataji (2020) and Goto and Watanabe (2021).

Discussion Mice learned to select the larger of two dot arrays and showed evidence of transfer to several novel numerosity pairs.

After acquiring the 8-versus-4 discrimination, they performed above chance on several untrained comparisons involving both familiar and unfamiliar numerosities, although performance on the most difficult comparison, 8 versus 7, did not exceed chance.

This pattern of transfer is consistent with previous demonstrations of approximate numerosity discrimination in nonhuman animals using two-choice paradigms, including rats tested with visual arrays (Cox & Montrose, 2016) and striped field mice (Reznikova et al., 2019).

Performance varied systematically as a function of numerical ratio, and accuracy decreased as the numerical ratio approached 1.0, a pattern consistent with Weber-like scaling.
The relation between numerical ratio and discrimination accuracy was similar across Tests 1 and 2, indicating that ratio-dependent performance generalized across both test formats.

text.text: The control manipulations provided further insight into the perceptual basis of this discrimination.
When filled dots were replaced with open circles (Test 4), performance remained above chance across all numerical pairs, although it was weakest for the largest numerosity pair.

When dot size was adjusted to equate cumulative surface area between arrays (Test 5), performance fell to chance or below-chance levels for most comparisons, suggesting that cumulative area likely served as a supporting cue in the earlier tests.
Disrupting discrete item structure through phase scrambling (Test 6) also impaired performance.

Mice did not perform above chance for the larger pairs, indicating that the global luminance and spatial-frequency information preserved by phase scrambling was not sufficient to support those discriminations.

By contrast, performance remained above chance for 4 versus 2 and 2 versus 1, suggesting that some residual nonnumerical information preserved in the scrambled displays was sufficient to guide choice for these smaller pairs.

Thus, Test 6 should not be interpreted as showing preserved numerosity-based discrimination for the smaller pairs, but rather as evidence that performance was sensitive to discrete item structure and to additional visual information that remained available after scrambling.

Although the phase-scrambled condition was included primarily as a control for discrete item structure, it is also theoretically relevant because the two cerebral hemispheres have been proposed to differ in their sensitivity to spatial-frequency information, which may contribute to spatial-numerical associations (Felisatti et al., 2020).

text.text: Experiment 2 examined whether side choice varied systematically with probe numerosity under equal-equal conditions in which reinforcement was independent of left-right responding.
The results showed a positive linear relation between probe numerosity and the probability of choosing the left side, suggesting a magnitude-related spatial bias under the present task conditions.
However, this pattern was stronger at the level of the overall linear trend than at the level of individual probe numerosities or individual subjects and should therefore be interpreted cautiously.
Baseline 8 versus 4 trials also did not show a significant overall side bias, suggesting that the probe pattern did not simply reflect a preexisting left-right preference.

This finding is broadly consistent with previous reports that numerical magnitude can influence spatial biases in nonhuman animals, although the direction and strength of such effects vary across species and procedures (Gazes et al., 2017; Johnson-Ulrich & Vonk, 2018; Lazareva et al., 2020; Jackson et al., 2026).

text.text: A strength of the present design is that reinforcement on probe trials was noncontingent with respect to side choice, reducing the likelihood that the observed pattern reflected direct reinforcement of left or right responses during the probes.

However, because the same mice were tested in Experiment 2 after completing Experiment 1, the present design cannot determine whether the observed magnituderelated spatial bias reflects an innate predisposition, an association acquired through prior experience, or an interaction between the two.

text.text: Importantly, the choose-larger training contingency did not systematically favor either spatial location and therefore does not, by itself, explain the direction of the observed bias.
Thus, although prior learning may have influenced spatial responding, its contribution remains unknown.
The present study addressed two related questions about magnitude processing in mice using static visual dot arrays.

First, Experiment 1 examined whether mice could extract behaviorally relevant magnitude information from such displays, as indicated by transfer to novel comparisons, ratiodependent performance, and sensitivity to non-numerical control manipulations.

The results showed that mice learned a relative numerosity discrimination and generalized it beyond the training pair, but also that performance was influenced by visual properties correlated with numerosity, particularly under more demanding stimulus conditions.
Experiment 2 then tested whether this information influenced side choice when identical dot arrays were presented simultaneously on the left and right and neither side was designated as correct.
Under those probe conditions, the probability of left-side choice increased with numerosity.

Taken together, these findings suggest that mice can extract behaviorally relevant magnitude information from static dot arrays and that this information can, under the present task conditions, bias lateralized choice.
The results of Experiment 1 extend previous work on numerosity processing in mice by demonstrating relative numerosity discrimination from simultaneously presented static arrays.

Previous work has established that mice can process numerosity-like information with scalar variability, but those findings have come predominantly from sequential or response-based paradigms (Berkay et al., 2016; Çavdaroğlu & Balcı, 2016; Gür et al., 2021; Light et al., 2019) rather than simultaneous visual comparisons.

text.text: Control manipulations highlighted how continuous visual dimensions contributed to discrimination.
Replacing filled dots with open circles left performance above chance across all numerosity pairs, although it was weakest for the largest numerosity pair.
Equating cumulative surface area or disrupting discrete item structure through phase scrambling generally reduced accuracy, although the effects differed across numerosity pairs.
Taken together, these findings indicate that mice did not rely on numerosity in isolation.
Rather, their performance was influenced by visual properties correlated with numerosity, such as total area and spatial structure.

A similar pattern has been reported in wolves and dogs tested with simultaneously presented dot arrays in a touchscreen paradigm: although performance followed Weber's law, control analyses suggested that choices were also supported by continuous nonnumerical cues, including stimulus size and shape (Rivas-Blanco et al., 2020).

text.text: This convergence suggests that ratio-dependent performance and reliance on correlated visual information are not mutually exclusive in comparative numerosity tasks.

The spatial bias was observed after the mice had completed discrimination training in which numerosity was behaviorally relevant but in which continuous visual dimensions also contributed to performance.
Accordingly, the probe result is best interpreted as evidence that magnitude-related information, rather than necessarily numerosity alone, biased side choice.
Under these conditions, larger magnitudes were associated with a higher probability of left-side choice.

text.text: Here, the mice were trained on a relative numerosity rule rather than on a single reference value, and spatial bias was assessed as a function of absolute numerosity.

This design was well suited to detecting monotonic, magnitude-dependent modulation of side choice under conditions with minimal explicit spatial contingencies, but it does not test the referencedependent reversals that are central to some anchor-based accounts.
An additional probe reported in the Supplementary Materials showed a directionally similar trend when dot positions were randomized (Figure S2), providing preliminary support for the main effect.

text.text: However, because the supplementary effect was weaker and equal-equal probe procedures have yielded mixed results across species (Beran et al., 2019; Triki & Bshary, 2018), further replication will be needed to establish the reliability and boundary conditions of this pattern.

text.text: Several limitations constrain the generality of the present findings.
All mice were trained to choose the larger numerosity.
Accordingly, the present findings show that mice can acquire and generalize a choose-larger discrimination, but they do not establish equivalent learning under a choosesmaller rule.

Because previous research suggests that numerosity discrimination can be asymmetric across reward contingencies, whether the same pattern would emerge in the present touchscreen task remains an open question (Inman et al., 2015; Lazareva et al., 2020).
text.formatted: Because previous research suggests that numerosity discrimination can be asymmetric across reward contingencies, whether the same pattern would emerge in the present touchscreen task remains an open question <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">(Inman et al., 2015;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">Lazareva et al., 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Because all mice had extensive prior discrimination training, the present study cannot determine whether the magnitude-related sidechoice bias was present before training or emerged through experience.

Although stimulus control was improved relative to many earlier rodent studies, numerosity and continuous visual dimensions were not fully decorrelated across all conditions, limiting direct comparison with human SNARC effects.
Moreover, the small sample size and substantial individual variability, including opposite trends in two of the six mice, limit the generalizability of the group-level effect.
Despite these limitations, the present findings have broader significance.

At the behavioral level, they show that mice can learn and generalize relative numerosity discrimination from static visual arrays and exhibit ratio-dependent performance in a simultaneous visual comparison task.
They also show that, following training on relative numerosity discrimination, side choice can vary systematically with stimulus magnitude under noncontingent probe conditions.
Methodologically, these findings support the use of mice as a promising model for investigating how magnitude-related information extracted from visual displays guides choice.

Because mice are well suited to neural recording and targeted manipulation, this paradigm provides a foundation for identifying the neural mechanisms that support relative numerosity discrimination and magnitude-dependent spatial bias.
